title: Yesterday
job: Past tense — the first big divergence
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: English has one simple past and Spanish has two, and the choice is not "finished" against "unfinished" — both of them are finished. It is how the event is PRESENTED: the preterite presents it as one bounded whole (Ayer comí pan), the imperfect presents it as an open frame — a habit that used to run, or a state that was simply going on (Antes comía pan · Ayer estaba ocupado).

The preterite's "I" ending is -é for the -ar family and -í for the -er and -ir families: hablé, trabajé, estudié · comí, escribí. Both are stressed, and both are written with the accent that proves it.
The accent IS the tense. hablo (I speak) · hablé (I spoke) · habló (he spoke) differ by nothing else at all. Leave the mark off hablé and you have written the present.
The imperfect's "I" ending is -aba for the -ar family and -ía for the -er and -ir families: hablaba, trabajaba · comía, vivía. This is the form behind English's "used to".

ayer names one bounded day, so it usually pulls the preterite — Ayer comí pan. antes opens a stretch of time with no edges, so it pulls the imperfect — Antes comía pan. Usually, not always: Ayer estaba ocupado uses the imperfect for a state the whole day sat in.
One word, two verbs: fui is the past of ir ("I went") and the past of ser ("I was"). Nothing inside it chooses — what follows does. Fui a México is went; Fui estudiante is was.

The everyday irregular pasts are learned whole rather than by rule: hice (I did, I made) · hiciste (you did) · fui (I went, I was) · tuve (I had) · estuve (I was). None of them carries a written accent, which is itself the sign that they are irregular.

M2's split survives into the past: era is ser (what someone WAS — Antes era estudiante) and estaba is estar (what state they were IN — Ayer estaba ocupado). Both are also "he or she was"; the sentence says which.

An adjective in the past agrees with the SUBJECT exactly as it does in the present: Ayer estaba ocupado (a man about himself) · Ayer estaba ocupada (a woman) · ¿Estabas ocupada? (asked of a woman). The tense changes and the agreement does not.

Negation does not move for the past. no still goes straight in front of the verb and the verb keeps the tense: Ayer no trabajé. English shifts the past onto a helper — "did not work" — and Spanish has no helper to shift it onto.
"I ate" and "I have eaten" both come out as comí once ayer is in the sentence. Spanish does have a compound past, but a finished yesterday is not where it goes.

words.note: Yesterday. It usually opens the sentence, and it is what tells you the verb behind it has moved into the past.
comer in the preterite: one meal as one finished event. The -í is the preterite "I" of the -er and -ir families and takes the stress — co-MÍ, against M4's CO-mo. Also comiste (you), comió (he, she).

sentences.trap: English can say "I ate" or "I have eaten" and mean the same afternoon. With ayer, Spanish takes the preterite and only the preterite: Ayer comí pan.
sentences.sound: co-MÍ. The accent drags the stress to the end, and that is the entire difference from como.

variations.changed: swap what you ate
no in front of the verb, as ever
-í → -iste and the question turns to you

mistake.why: como is the present. Yesterday needs comí — the accent is the tense.

sentences.usage: The first thing anyone asks about yesterday.
sentences.mnemonic: The accent walks to the end and the verb walks into the past.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I spoke with my sister

words.note: hablar in the preterite. The -ar family takes -é for "I": hablé, trabajé, estudié. The other persons are hablaste (you) and habló (he, she, usted) — hablo, hablé, habló are three words one mark apart.

sentences.trap: hablé and habló are one accent apart, and the accent decides who did the talking: hablé is I, habló is he or she.
sentences.sound: a-BLÉ — silent h, and the stress on the last syllable where the accent puts it.

variations.changed: swap who you spoke to
a language goes straight after hablar, with no con
-é → -ó: the same past with someone else doing the talking

mistake.why: Without the accent it is the present. Yesterday takes hablé.

words.note: trabajar in the preterite — the same -é ending as hablé, and the stress lands on it: tra-ba-JÉ. The rest of the family runs the same way: trabajaste (you) · trabajó (he, she, usted).

sentences.trap: English moves the past onto a helper — did not work — and leaves the verb looking present. Spanish keeps the past on the verb and puts a bare no in front: Ayer no trabajé.
sentences.sound: tra-ba-JÉ. The j rasps from the back of the throat and the é is the loudest syllable.

variations.cue: Yesterday I worked in the morning
variations.changed: the affirmative, with a time phrase from M4
swap the verb — the frame holds
-é → -aste, and the marks make it a question

mistake.why: trabajo is the present. Yesterday needs trabajé.

sentences.mnemonic: no in front, the past on the verb.

words.note: hacer, "to do" and "to make", in the preterite: hice (I did) · hiciste (you did) · hizo (he, she, usted did). A strong past, so no written accent. Both negatives stay: no … nada.

sentences.trap: M3's double negative, now in the past: No hice nada is "I didn't do anything", and neither half of it can be dropped.
sentences.sound: I-ce. The h is silent, and the c before an e is an s across Latin America and a th in most of Spain.

variations.changed: the opposite answer, with M1's mucho
drop ayer and it stretches to any day you like
hice → hiciste: the same empty day, handed to you

mistake.why: hacer does not take the regular ending: the past is hice.

sentences.usage: The honest answer to what you did yesterday.
sentences.mnemonic: hice is short because it is irregular — no accent, no rule.

words.note: hacer in the preterite for tú: hice (I did) · hiciste (you did). No written accent on either of them, and the stress is in the middle: i-CIS-te. One word for "did do".

sentences.trap: English needs "did" AND the plain verb. Spanish carries both in one word, and the question keeps the order a statement would have.
sentences.sound: i-CIS-te — silent h again, and no accent to mark the stress because it falls where it is expected.

variations.cue: What did you do in the morning?
variations.changed: narrow it to one part of the day
add the name after a comma
hiciste → hizo: the question moves to a third person

mistake.why: Drop the tú — hiciste already says "you did".

sentences.usage: The question that starts the conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: hice and hiciste — one pair, no accents.

words.note: One word doing the past of two verbs: ir ("I went") and ser ("I was"). What follows decides — Fui a México is went, Fui estudiante is was. A strong past, so no accent; fui · fuiste · fue.

sentences.trap: It reads as ambiguous and is not. A destination after fui makes it "went"; a role or a description makes it "was". This is also M4's a in its third seat — pointing at a place.
sentences.sound: One syllable, FWEE: the u and the i run together and nothing is stressed apart from them.

variations.changed: swap the destination
no destination, so the same word means "I was"
fui → fue: her trip, not yours

mistake.why: A destination needs the a in front of it: fui a México.

sentences.mnemonic: fui went and fui was — look at what comes after it.

words.note: estudiar in the preterite — the fourth shape of one verb: estudiante (the person), estudiar, estudio (I study), estudié (I studied). Other persons follow hablé's: estudiaste · estudió.

sentences.trap: estudio and estudié are the same stem with one letter and one mark between them, and that mark is the day you are talking about.
sentences.sound: es-tu-DIÉ, stressed on the last syllable — the accent is there to say so.

variations.changed: name what you studied
the double negative, in the past
-é → -ó: someone else did the studying

mistake.why: Without the accent it is the present. Yesterday is estudié.

sentences.usage: Reporting effort — the answer to ¿Qué hiciste ayer?

sentences.display: Antes comía pan todos los días
sentences.cue: I used to eat bread every day
sentences.literal: Before I-was-eating bread all the days

words.note: "Before", in the sense of "in those days". It opens a stretch of past time with no edges rather than pointing at one day, which is why the verb after it is usually the imperfect.
comer in the imperfect: "I used to eat", "I was eating". The -er and -ir families take -ía. Beside comí — one meal, closed — it presents the eating as an open frame. comía is both I and he or she.

sentences.trap: Both sentences are about time that is over. Antes comía pan and Ayer comí pan differ in how the eating is presented, not in whether it has finished.
sentences.sound: co-MÍ-a is three syllables: the accent splits the i from the a and keeps the stress on it.

variations.cue: I used to eat a lot of bread
variations.changed: add M1's mucho
one day, one meal — so the preterite comes back

variations.cue: Did you use to eat bread?
variations.changed: comía → comías — the used-to question, aimed at you

mistake.display: Antes comí pan todos los días
mistake.why: With antes the eating is a stretch of time rather than an event, so Spanish reaches for the imperfect: Antes comía pan todos los días.

sentences.usage: Talking about how things used to be.

sentences.cue: I used to be a student

words.cue: I was · he was · she was
words.note: ser in the imperfect — "I used to be", and equally "he or she was": one shape for both, and the sentence decides. tú takes eras. It says what someone WAS, where estaba says what state they were in.

sentences.trap: era and fui are both "I was". Fui estudiante packages the whole stretch as one closed chapter; Antes era estudiante leaves it open as the way things used to be.
sentences.sound: E-ra, stressed on the first syllable, and the single r is one light tap.

variations.cue: I used to be a music student
variations.changed: say what of — de links the two nouns, as in M1
the very same form, now about someone else
no in front of era — the used-to state, denied

mistake.why: Being a student is what you are, not a state you are in: Antes era estudiante.

sentences.usage: Saying what you used to be.
sentences.mnemonic: era for who you were, estaba for how you were.

words.cue: I was · he was · she was
words.note: estar in the imperfect — the past of M2's estoy, and the same shape for "he or she was", with estabas for tú. It takes the kind of word estoy took: estaba bien, estaba ocupado. Said by a man: ocupado.

sentences.trap: ayer usually pulls the preterite, and here it does not: a state that simply held all day is presented as a frame. Ayer estuve ocupado is also said — that one packages the day as a single closed block.
sentences.sound: es-TA-ba. The b between vowels is soft, nearer an English v than a b.

variations.cue: Yesterday I was busy (a woman speaking)
variations.changed: -o → -a: the ending follows the subject in the past exactly as in the present
no in front of the verb, and the tense stays put

variations.cue: Were you busy yesterday? (asked of a man)
variations.changed: estaba → estabas, and ocupado still follows the man being asked

mistake.why: Being busy is a state, so it takes estar: Ayer estaba ocupado. era would be saying it was what you were.

sentences.mnemonic: estoy today, estaba yesterday — same verb, same job.
